abstract: San Francisco Fed economists ask whether the US has entered a high-productivity-growth era. GDP grew about 2.5% a year over three years with near-zero employment growth, and labor productivity rose solidly while utilization-adjusted TFP lagged. A regime-switching model puts the probability of a high-growth regime at about 57% using labor productivity and 21% using TFP as of Q4 2025 — neither a definitive signal. The divergence suggests AI-related investment is making workers more productive through capital deepening, while broader efficiency gains remain unrealized. Re-running the model with data only through 1997 shows the 1990s boom looked similarly ambiguous in real time, which the authors read as grounds for cautious optimism.
keyFindings: ~57% probability of a high-productivity-growth regime using labor productivity, Q4 2025
US output grew ~2.5% a year over three years with near-zero employment growth
Labor productivity–TFP divergence points to capital deepening from AI investment, not broad efficiency gains
Mid-1990s regime probabilities looked similarly mixed in real time before the boom became clear
methodology: Regime-switching model (Foerster and Matthes 2022) applied to US business-sector labor productivity and utilization-adjusted TFP (Fernald 2014), with a real-time counterfactual using data only through 1997.
qualifiers: Fed research letter (repo convention: Tier 1). Model-based probabilities, not forecasts of AI's contribution. Views are the authors', not the Federal Reserve's. Explicitly declines to claim a regime shift has occurred.
